title: The Course Correction
primary_metric: fuel cost (USD) per nautical mile of net progress toward the rendezvous point (NDBC Data Buoy 44090)

options.A: The True Line — steer the vector-corrected heading, burning more fuel per hour to hold the shortest real-distance track
options.B: The Steady Burn — steer the uncorrected direct heading at economical throttle, burning less fuel per hour but drifting off the line as the current pushes the ship over the transit

sources.claim: Measured ocean current, direction and speed, at NDBC Data Buoy 44090 (Cape Cod Bay, MA), shallowest depth bin
sources.value: Direction (toward) 340 deg T; speed 27 cm/s (0.5248 kt)
sources.title: Real-time ADCP data, station 44090
sources.note: Live real-time federal ocean-observation data, directly fetched (not a search snippet). Station location (41.840N, 70.329W) confirmed separately at https://www.ndbc.noaa.gov/station_page.php?station=44090. Depth bin: 1 m.

sources.claim: Speed/fuel-consumption figures for a real 110-foot coastal fisheries research vessel (R/V Medeia)
sources.value: 8.5 kt (1250 RPM) = 19 gal/hr; 9.5 kt (1460 RPM) = 32 gal/hr; ~11.5 kt (near top speed) = 60 gal/hr
sources.org: Alaska Department of Fish and Game
sources.title: "Medeia cuts fuel consumption 30 percent" (Wildlife News)
sources.note: Real, named, government-published vessel-operations figures for the R/V Medeia. Used as the sourced speed/fuel basis for the fictional Coastal Aster's 'coastal research-vessel class' spec, per the concept sheet's own guidance to use a stated, sourced-range spec rather than claim proprietary numbers for a named real ship the case did not independently verify. Article is from 2008; no more recent public fuel-curve figure for a comparable vessel class was found.

sources.title: U.S. No. 2 Diesel Retail Prices, weekly series
sources.note: Live federal price series, most recent published week at time of writing. On-highway/retail diesel used as a proxy for marine diesel price at this small a vessel scale, since no marine-specific bunker price index quotes at this scale publicly (Ship & Bunker's global average pages returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher and quote large-vessel bunker-scale MGO/VLSFO/IFO380 pricing, not small-craft retail diesel).

sources.claim: Whether NDBC reports ocean current direction as the direction the current flows FROM or TOWARD
sources.title: Nonstandard Meteorological/Ocean Data Measurement Descriptions
sources.note: Official NDBC documentation: 'The direction the ocean current is flowing toward.' Confirms the convention is the opposite of NDBC's own wind-direction convention (reported FROM), which is load-bearing for correctly resolving S1's current vector into components.

deliverables.text: A current-vector table: the measured current at Buoy 44090 as a magnitude and a direction, resolved into east and north components, with the full conversion (cm/s to kt, and the toward-convention resolution) shown.
A course unit-vector table: the desired course expressed as a unit vector (magnitude exactly one, shown), plus each option's heading vector as boat speed times a heading unit vector.

A resultant-velocity table for The Steady Burn: heading vector plus current vector (vector addition), then a dot product against the course unit vector to split the resultant into along-track and cross-track components, with a stated sign convention.

A vector diagram for each option, drawn to scale: heading, current, and resultant vectors added head to tail, with The True Line's correction (crab) angle and The Steady Burn's drift angle both labeled.

A fuel-cost table for both options (engine hours, fuel, dollar cost, dollars per net nautical mile) plus a statement, defended with D3's along-track component, of whether each option makes the weather window.

balance.argument_a: The True Line's vector-corrected heading puts the resultant exactly on the shortest real-distance line to Buoy 44090 -- zero wasted distance -- and it is the only option that reliably makes the 3.0-hour weather window (it is solved to make it with exactly zero slack; Option B misses it by about 22 minutes). The extra fuel cost is real but is bought at a specific, computable price: $15.99 per net nautical mile versus $13.29 for the uncorrected option, a 16.9% premium for both distance efficiency and a reliable on-time arrival.
balance.argument_b: The Steady Burn holds the ship's most fuel-efficient throttle setting -- the lowest fuel burn of any speed the ship can make -- for the entire transit, and still reaches the buoy: the extra ~1.67 nm the current drifts the ship off-line (about 6% more distance) costs far less, per net nautical mile, than the higher throttle The True Line requires. On the case's own primary metric it is the cheaper option by 16.9%, and the missed weather window is a real but separate cost -- a schedule risk against a 'tightest part of the window' framing, not a hard cutoff -- that a crew focused on the cruise's finite fuel budget may reasonably choose to accept.
balance.margin_basis: Fuel cost per net nautical mile for each option, computed from real sourced current data (S1), real sourced vessel speed/fuel data (S2), and a real sourced diesel price (S3), against the case's stated rendezvous geometry (MA1) and weather window (MA2). Option A's net progress equals the full 27.0 nm (it lands exactly on the buoy); Option B's net progress also equals 27.0 nm but only after an extra correction leg, so its cost is spread over a longer real distance sailed (28.67 nm) for the same net progress.
balance.winner: B — The Steady Burn (cheaper per net nautical mile)
balance.margin_pct_note: COMPUTED 2026-09-01 (case-research, sensitivity_model.py). Option A (The True Line): required speed-over-ground = 27.0 nm / 3.0 hr = 9.000 kt; solving Heading = DesiredResultant - Current (vector subtraction) for a resultant exactly on the 250.0 deg T course gives a required boat speed through the water of 9.0153 kt, interpolated fuel rate 25.699 gal/hr (MA3, between S2's real 8.5kt/19gph and 9.5kt/32gph points), time 3.0000 hr exactly (zero slack against the window), fuel 77.096 gal, cost $431.66 (at S3's $5.599/gal), metric = $431.66 / 27.0 nm = $15.9875/nm. Option B (The Steady Burn): heading vector at 8.5 kt (S2's economical point) on the uncorrected 250.0 deg T bearing, plus the current vector (S1), gives a resultant of 8.5162 kt at 253.53 deg T; dot product against the course unit vector splits this into an along-track rate of 8.5000 kt and a cross-track rate of 0.5248 kt; time to close 27.0 nm along-track = 3.1765 hr, at which point the ship is 1.6671 nm off-line (MA4's un-modeled final leg), adding 0.1961 hr at the same 8.5 kt to close that leg -- total time 3.3726 hr (22.4 min over the 3.0 hr window), engine distance 28.6671 nm, fuel 64.079 gal (at S2's 19 gal/hr economical rate), cost $358.78, metric = $358.78 / 27.0 nm = $13.2882/nm. margin_pct = (15.9875 - 13.2882) / 15.9875 x 100 = 16.88%. WINNER on the stated primary metric: Option B. This is comfortably under SPEC Section 2's ~20% cap -- no retune was needed. Full arithmetic trail and flex-sweep sensitivity in sensitivity_model.py and RESEARCH_LOG.md.

modeling_assumptions.claim: The Coastal Aster's distance and bearing to Buoy 44090 at the start of the watch
modeling_assumptions.value: 27.0 nm on a true course of 250.0 deg
modeling_assumptions.basis: Fictional ship position; chosen to put the buoy a realistic few hours away and to place the measured current at a working angle across the course (not dead ahead or dead abeam) so both along-track and cross-track effects show up.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH on distance (paired with MA2, sets Option A's required speed-over-ground -- flexing distance +-25%/+-50% flips the winner outside roughly -20%/+20%); MODERATE on bearing (flexing +-25deg/+-50deg moves margin_pct between ~3% and ~28% without flipping the winner in the tested range).

modeling_assumptions.claim: Hours remaining in the closing weather window
modeling_assumptions.basis: Matches the Overview's closing-front framing; a stated scenario deadline.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: HIGH -- enters Option A's required speed-over-ground inversely. Loosening the window flips the $/nm winner to Option A; the 3.0 hr base case sits close to that flip boundary.

modeling_assumptions.claim: Fuel consumption between two published Appendix C data points is found by linear interpolation
modeling_assumptions.value: Applied to The True Line's required ~9.015 kt setting
modeling_assumptions.basis: No published data point exists at exactly the required speed; linear interpolation between the two nearest real, sourced points is the most conservative choice without inventing a curve shape.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: LOW-MODERATE -- the required speed sits only 1.6% of the way from the low anchor to the mid anchor, so curve-shape choice barely moves the interpolated rate.

modeling_assumptions.claim: The Steady Burn's final correction leg is sailed at the same 8.5 kt economical throttle, current not separately modeled on that leg
modeling_assumptions.value: Applied to Option B's D5 fuel total
modeling_assumptions.basis: Simplification stated openly, matching Wind Triangle's per-leg constant-wind approach; the leg is short (1.67 nm of 27.0 nm, ~6% of the path).
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: LOW -- re-solving this short leg under the same current would change margin_pct by well under one percentage point.

sensitivity_note: margin_pct (16.88%) is comfortably under SPEC Section 2's ~20% cap, but the scenario constraints that produce it (MA1's distance, MA2's weather-window hours) are themselves highly load-bearing: together they set Option A's required speed-over-ground (27.0 nm / 3.0 hr = 9.000 kt), which decides which part of the real, sourced Appendix C fuel curve Option A has to buy. sensitivity_model.py's flex sweep shows the cheaper-per-nm winner flips from B to A if the window loosens by roughly 25% or more (holding distance fixed), or if the distance shortens by roughly 20-25% or more (holding the window fixed) -- i.e. this is a genuinely close, genuinely sensitive case, not an artificially close one masking a lopsided real result. The bearing component of MA1 and the interpolation/final-leg modeling choices (MA3, MA4) are comparatively minor levers. See FACILITATOR.md and sensitivity_model.py for the full computed margin and flex sweep.
